newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine court confirms 11 indicted in IBM case.
newsitem.headline: Argentine court confirms 11 indicted in IBM case.

text.p: An Argentine court confirmed the indictment of 11 people in an investigation into possible bribes paid to ensure that the local unit of IBM won a $250 million deal to install a computer system at a state bank, the investigating judge said on Tuesday.

"On Monday, the Federal Court also lifted the indictment I had ordered against another 19 people," Judge Adolfo Bagnasco told Reuters. "This means a partial confirmation of my decision. I will keep investigating."

Last April, Bagnasco indicted 30 Argentine government officials and former officials of International Business Machines Corp's Argentine unit as part of an investigation into a 1993 contract to upgrade computers at Banco Nacion.
He added that he could prove there was embezzlement, but not that bribes were paid.

The judge suspects millions of dollars in bribes were paid through IBM Argentina's subcontractors. Among the indictments confirmed by the court are those of former Banco Nacion head Aldo Dadone, former IBM Argentina President Ricardo Martorana and ex-Vice-President Gustavo Soriani.

Banco Nacion cancelled the deal in June and demanded that IBM Argentina refund $82 million in payments, but the company fired back, suing the bank in July for more then $86 million alleging "wrongful revocation" of the contract.

Then in August, Banco Nacion sued the firm for $174 million and asked courts to declare the contract "null and void." The firm has denied any malicious intent, although it has admitted to errors. Other IBM Argentina deals are under separate investigation.

Another Argentine judge said there were "serious irregularities" both in the $425 million cost and the direct awarding by decree of a contract between IBM Argentina and the country's tax collection body DGI.
Yet another judge is investigating why a deal between IBM Argentina and the government of the western province of Mendoza was awarded by decree instead of by tender.
